rows.label: Concept
rows.text: The mineral diet splits by **daily requirement**. **Macro-nutrients (>100 mg/day):** Ca, P, K, S, Na, Cl, Mg — structure (Ca/P bones), electrolytes (Na/K/Cl nerves and fluids), chlorophyll (Mg) and proteins (S). **Micro-nutrients (<100 mg/day):** Fe, Zn, Cu, I, Co, Mn, Mo, Cr, Se, F — the catalytic and hormonal tier.…

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: "Iodine is essential for the formation of thyroxine; its deficiency causes goitre, which can be prevented by using iodised salt."

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***Iodised salt, chemistry's cheapest public-health win*** — adding a pinch of KIO3/KI to NaCl supplies the ~150 ug of iodine the thyroid needs and removes goitre from whole countries.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — Grams versus Micrograms Nutrition divides the inorganic diet into two weight classes. **Macro-nutrients (macro-minerals)** are needed in amounts of more than about 100 mg per day — Ca, P, K, S, Na, Cl, Mg. **Micro-nutrients (trace elements)** are needed in less than 100 mg per day — Fe, Zn, Cu, I, Co, Mn, Mo, Cr, Se, F — yet a shortage of any one of them produces a named deficiency…  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts ### 2.1 The macro-minerals (7 of them) - **Ca** — bones and teeth, muscle contraction, blood clotting, nerve signalling. - **P** — bones (with Ca), ATP and nucleic acids, energy currency. - **K** — principal intracellular cation; nerve impulses, enzyme activation. - **Na** — principal extracellular cation; fluid balance, nerve impulses. - **Cl** — gastric HCl, electrolyte balance.…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Macro 7: Ca-P-K-S-Na-Cl-Mg. Trace: Fe-Zn-Cu-I-Co-Mn-Mo-Cr-Se-F. Disease pairs: Fe-anaemia, I-goitre, Co-B12-pernicious anaemia, Mg-chlorosis. Iodine dose ~150 ug/day; fix = iodised salt.

(a) zinc (b) copper (c) iron (d) iodine** — **(c) iron.** Each of the four haem groups of haemoglobin carries an Fe²⁺ ion that reversibly binds one O₂ molecule; iron deficiency therefore lowers…

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: The iodine answer needs three parts — hormone (thyroxine), disorder (goitre) and preventive measure (iodised salt); omitting the preventive measure loses the last mark.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: The macro/trace divide is a divide of quantity, not importance: iron runs the entire oxygen economy on a few grams, iodine sets the metabolic rate on ~150 micrograms — and each missing microgram has a named disease.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Macro-nutrients: needed >100 mg/day — Ca, P, K, S, Na, Cl, Mg (Ca bones/clotting, P ATP/DNA, K-Na nerve impulses, Cl HCl, Mg chlorophyll, S proteins). Micro-nutrients: <100 mg/day — Fe, Zn, Cu, I, Co, Mn, Mo, Cr, Se, F.…

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Iron is the most abundant trace metal in the human body (~4 g), almost all of it in haemoglobin and myoglobin; the body recycles it so efficiently that daily dietary need is only about 1-2 mg.

Detailed Explanation ### 4.1 Why the 100 mg line matters - The macro/trace division is about **daily requirement**, not importance. Na⁺ and K⁺ must be replaced in grams because the body leaks them constantly; Fe must be supplied in milligrams because it is recycled almost perfectly. Losing a trace element hurts just as much — it simply takes longer to run out.…  ·  ## 5. rows.text: Distinguish iron-deficiency anaemia from pernicious anaemia by naming the metal and vitamin involved in each.  ·  ## 6. Common Confusions **Macro-nutrient ≠ protein/carb/fat here:** in this chemistry unit "macro-nutrients" means the mineral elements Ca–Mg, not the energy foods; the food-group sense belongs to biology.  ·  **Cobalt deficiency causes anaemia indirectly:** Co is not in haemoglobin — it is in vitamin B₁₂, which is needed to make red blood cells. Iron anaemia and B₁₂ (pernicious) anaemia are different diseases.
